questions.title: Under FOIA Exemption 7(A), do "enforcement proceedings" include ongoing criminal investigations, or must there be a filed case?
questions.question_body: The panel says "ongoing criminal investigations count as 'proceedings'" and that the government may show such proceedings by attesting to their "existence" (citing CREW and Juarez). I'm confused because the statute says disclosure that could reasonably be expected to interfere with enforcement proceedings. Does an open-ended counterterrorism investigation, without charges filed, qualify? How "concrete" must a prospective proceeding be to satisfy 7(A), and what distinguishes a general intelligence/information-gathering operation from a qualifying enforcement proceeding?

questions.title: How does de novo review square with the court’s deference to the FBI’s national-security judgments in FOIA cases?
questions.question_body: The opinion says summary judgment is reviewed de novo and the government bears the burden, but also that the FBI’s invocation of Exemption 7 gets deference, especially where national security is implicated (citing Campbell and CNSS). What exactly is being reviewed de novo versus what gets deference? Is the court deferring to predictive judgments about harm while independently verifying the legal standards are met? How far does that deference go when key details are in ex parte declarations?

questions.title: Is the opinion’s citation to 5 U.S.C. § 552(b)(7)(B) a typo when discussing Exemption 7(A)?
questions.question_body: In Section IV.B, the court quotes the interference-with-proceedings standard but cites § 552(b)(7)(B). My understanding is that (b)(7)(A) is the interference-with-enforcement-proceedings exemption, while (b)(7)(B) concerns fair trial rights. Is this just a scrivener’s error, and does it have any legal consequence for the holding?

questions.title: When do FOIA declarations become too "stale," and what obligates an agency to update them?
questions.question_body: The district court initially denied summary judgment without prejudice due to the passage of time and required an updated assessment on whether proceedings were still pending or reasonably anticipated. Are there established D.C. Circuit benchmarks for when agency declarations become stale in 7(A) cases? What factors (e.g., years elapsed, nature of investigation, prior confirmations) trigger a duty to supplement, and is that duty grounded in FOIA, summary-judgment standards, or the court’s inherent authority?

questions.title: Can a court properly find no reasonably segregable material based solely on ex parte submissions?
questions.question_body: The district court relied on Bender’s supplemental ex parte declaration to conclude there was no reasonably segregable information, and the D.C. Circuit approved that approach (citing Perioperative Services). What must an agency show, even ex parte, to meet its segregability burden? Is there a minimum level of public explanation (e.g., a Vaughn index or categorical description) required before a court can rely entirely on sealed specifics? How do courts ensure that "meaningful" nonexempt information isn’t overlooked when the adversary can’t test the assertions?

questions.title: Did the FOIA Improvement Act’s foreseeable-harm requirement add anything beyond Exemption 7(A)’s own harm standard here?
questions.question_body: FOIA’s 2016 amendments require agencies to show reasonably foreseeable harm from disclosure unless disclosure is prohibited by law. Exemption 7(A) already asks whether release "could reasonably be expected to interfere" with enforcement proceedings. Does the D.C. Circuit treat the foreseeable-harm requirement as coextensive with the 7(A) standard, or as an additional independent showing? I didn’t see a separate foreseeable-harm analysis—was it subsumed, or is there circuit precedent that a proper 7(A) showing satisfies the FOIA Improvement Act by itself?

questions.title: What suffices to show records were "compiled for law enforcement purposes," and may the court rely on allegations from separate immigration proceedings?
questions.question_body: The court invokes Pratt/Campbell’s "rational nexus" test and says broader context—including allegations presented in Farahi’s immigration case (e.g., ties to designated terrorist organizations and individuals)—confirms the law-enforcement purpose. Is it proper for the court to consider those allegations from another proceeding to bolster the nexus, especially when the detailed basis is in ex parte declarations? How specific must the public record be about a subject’s connection to a possible violation to meet Pratt without revealing sensitive details?

questions.title: Can Exemption 7(A) justify withholding for decades, and what recourse does a requester have as time passes?
questions.question_body: This investigation seems to date back many years, and the court accepts that it remains ongoing. Is there any temporal limit on 7(A) withholdings, or can they effectively persist indefinitely if an investigation never formally closes? If a requester suspects the "ongoing" status is outdated, is the remedy just to refile a new FOIA request later, or can courts require periodic updates or in camera review to test the continued applicability of 7(A)?
